title: Poolside at Peak Hour
objective: Assess guest safety at leisure facilities and choose proportionate controls.
subject: Pool safety review before the holidays
briefing: School holidays start next week and occupancy will hit 95%. I want a quick risk review of the pools at our resort properties.

documents.title: Pool observations
documents.body:
- Lifeguard cover 10:00-16:00 only; peak family use is 16:00-19:00.
- Depth markings faded at the shallow end.
- Two near misses last summer: a child struggling in the deep end at 17:30; a guest slipping on wet tiles.
- Rescue equipment present and checked daily.

options.text: No lifeguard cover during peak family hours

options.why: Diving injuries are often linked to unclear depth.

options.text: Extend lifeguard cover to 19:00 during holidays and repaint depth markings this week.

options.feedback: Safe but hurts guest experience; better to staff the peak.
This choice leaves the core exposure unmanaged and is likely to make things worse. A stronger option was: “Extend lifeguard cover to 19:00 during holidays and repaint depth markings this week.”

steps.prompt: Rate residual risk of a serious guest injury after your recommendation.
steps.why: With supervision at peak times and clear markings, likelihood drops to Rare; severity remains Severe.

debrief.summary: You targeted controls at the real exposure window.
key_points: Match controls to when the risk peaks.
Severity stays high even when likelihood falls.
debrief.stronger_approach: Add a near-miss log at each pool.
debrief.transfer: Peak-time exposure applies to crowd safety in stadiums and transport hubs.

endings.title: Strong outcome
endings.text: Your work set a high standard. Stakeholders now come to you early.

endings.title: Adequate outcome
endings.text: Solid work with gaps. Your manager asks you to revisit one or two points.

endings.title: Needs rework
endings.text: The work needs another pass. Use the debrief and try again when ready.

title: Fire Safety Inspection
objective: Prepare for a fire safety inspection: test controls, prioritise fixes and avoid cosmetic compliance.
subject: The fire marshal visits in ten days
briefing: The fire marshal inspects our flagship property in ten days. I want us to be genuinely safe, not just tidy for the visit.

rows: Weekly tests logged; two weeks missing

steps.why: Fix ignition sources and fire spread first, then people readiness, then paperwork.

steps.prompt: A manager suggests back-filling the missing alarm test entries.

options.text: No: record the gap honestly, test now, and fix the schedule.
options.feedback: Falsifying records is far worse than a gap.

options.text: Back-fill them; the tests probably happened.

steps.prompt: Night-shift drills are hard to run without disturbing guests. What do you propose?

options.text: A staff-only night drill with walk-throughs of guest evacuation roles, plus a desktop exercise.

options.feedback: This choice leaves the core exposure unmanaged and is likely to make things worse. A stronger option was: “A staff-only night drill with walk-throughs of guest evacuation roles, plus a desktop exercise.”

debrief.summary: You fixed real hazards first and kept records honest.
key_points: Fix ignition and spread before paperwork.
debrief.stronger_approach: Make fire-door failures a monthly KRI.
debrief.transfer: Inspection readiness without window-dressing applies to every regulator.

title: Cards at the Front Desk
objective: Assess payment card data risk in hotel systems and prioritise scope reduction.
subject: Card data risk at the front desk
briefing: Our card scheme assessment is due. Front-desk staff share logins and we still have old terminals at three properties. Where's the real exposure?

documents.title: Findings
documents.body:
- Shared front-desk logins at 9 of 16 properties.
- Legacy terminals (no encryption) at 3 properties, about 12% of card volume.
- Card numbers written on paper for phone bookings at two properties.
- Point-to-point encryption on all other terminals.

steps.prompt: How do you explain scope reduction to the GM?

options.text: The safest card data is data we never see: encrypted terminals and payment links remove card numbers from our systems and paperwork.

options.feedback: This choice leaves the core exposure unmanaged and is likely to make things worse. A stronger option was: “The safest card data is data we never see: encrypted terminals and payment links remove card numbers from our systems and paperwork.”

debrief.summary: You prioritised removing card data over protecting it everywhere.
key_points: Paper is a data channel too.
debrief.transfer: Data minimisation is the same principle in privacy and health records.

title: Hurricane Season
objective: Prepare business continuity for a coastal hotel portfolio: impact analysis, evacuation triggers and recovery priorities.
subject: Hurricane season starts in three weeks
briefing: Three of our coastal properties sit in the hurricane cone most years. I want a continuity plan that actually tells managers what to do and when.

documents.title: Last season
documents.body: Keys Resort evacuated late because the decision trigger was unclear; guests were stranded overnight in the lobby.

steps.prompt: What evacuation trigger do you propose?

options.text: Pre-agreed triggers by forecast category and time-to-landfall, with authority delegated to the GM, not head office.
Head office decides case by case.

options.feedback: This choice leaves the core exposure unmanaged and is likely to make things worse. A stronger option was: “Pre-agreed triggers by forecast category and time-to-landfall, with authority delegated to the GM, not head office.”

steps.prompt: Keys Resort's generator lasts 12h; outages last 36h on average. How many extra hours of fuel cover are needed?

debrief.summary: You set clear triggers and recovery priorities.
key_points: Size fuel to realistic outage durations.
debrief.stronger_approach: Run a tabletop exercise with GMs before the season.
debrief.transfer: Natural-hazard continuity applies to plants, hospitals and data centres.
